title: How Freedom of the Press Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and state of freedom of the press, starting with the printing press and seditious and blasphemous libel laws, then Trenchard and Gordon's Cato's Letters, the Zenger trial (1735), Sweden's 1766 Freedom of the Press Act, Virginia's charter language, the Sedition Acts of 1798 and 1918, Holmes and Brandeis's free speech opinions and the marketplace of ideas, New York Times v. Sullivan and actual malice, the Pentagon Papers case, press controls in China and Russia, self-censorship after 9/11, advertiser and corporate influence on journalism, social media, and the Gawker/Hulk Hogan lawsuit. They note the US ranks 44th of 180 in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index. The episode closes with a listener mail about rhinoplasty surgery.

segments.title: Opening and press freedom rankings
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and cite Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, where the US ranks 44th of 180 countries and Finland is first. They frame a free press as a pillar of democracy.

segments.title: Early printing press and seditious libel
segments.summary: After the fifteenth-century printing press spread, governments tried to control printed works through licensing and criminal laws. England's seditious and blasphemous libel laws made even true criticism of the government or church punishable.

segments.title: Cato's Letters and early free speech ideas
segments.summary: Trenchard and Gordon, writing as Cato in the colonies in the early 1720s, argued that free speech and public discussion were essential, that criticism of private failings was wrong, and that even opponents deserve free speech. Hosts note the importance of an informed public.

segments.title: Zenger trial of 1735
segments.summary: John Peter Zenger was jailed for about ten months for libel after printing attacks on New York's governor, William Cosby. He was acquitted after Andrew Hamilton convinced the jury to disregard the law, despite a compromised judge.

segments.title: Sweden and Virginia press freedom milestones
segments.summary: Sweden passed the first Freedom of the Press Act in 1766, which still put censorship duties on publishers and gave citizens access to government documents. Virginia's charter included language calling press freedom a bulwark of liberty.
topics: Sweden Freedom of the Press Act

segments.title: Sedition Act of 1798 and Jefferson's election
segments.summary: Congress passed the Sedition Act in 1798, criminalizing false, scandalous or malicious writing against the federal government. The Federalists who passed it lost power, and Jefferson became president.

segments.title: 1918 Sedition Act and Holmes and Brandeis
segments.summary: The 1918 Sedition Act and Espionage Act criminalized disloyal, abusive or anti-war speech, and close to two thousand people were prosecuted. Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes and Louis Brandeis developed free speech principles, including the marketplace of ideas.

segments.title: New York Times v. Sullivan and actual malice
segments.summary: In 1964 the Supreme Court overturned an Alabama ruling in a defamation suit by a police commissioner over a civil rights ad in the New York Times. The Court held that public officials must prove actual malice, not just factual error, for libel.

segments.title: Pentagon Papers and press controls abroad
segments.summary: Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers to the New York Times in 1971, and the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the government had not shown harm to national security. Hosts discuss the government never prosecuting a journalist for leaks and press control in China and Russia.

segments.title: Break and cliffhanger
segments.summary: Hosts take a break with a playful cliffhanger about a horse and parachutes.

segments.title: Self-censorship, advertisers, Gawker and social media
segments.summary: Hosts discuss self-censorship after 9/11, corporate and advertiser influence on reporting, the Gawker lawsuit funded by Peter Thiel and brought by Hulk Hogan, and social media's unclear ethical standards. They close by restating the US ranking.
